title: How do you work out percentages in your head quickly?
description: Percentages in your head: a quick way to do this case calculation in your head, with a worked example.
hook: Build every percentage from three blocks you can find instantly: 10% (move the decimal point one place), 5% (half of that) and 1% (move it two places). Any percentage in a case is a sum of those blocks, so you never need a calculator, and the method is hard to get wrong out loud.
body:
The method

What is 15% of 240?
  1. 10% of 240 is 24 (move the decimal point one place).
  2. 5% is half of that: 12.
  3. Add them: 24 + 12 = 36.

The same blocks build anything. 17.5% is 10% + 5% + 2.5% (half of 5%). 23% is 2 × 10% + 3 × 1%. 95% is 100% − 5%, which is often quicker than adding up: 95% of 680 is 680 − 34 = 646.

How to say it in the interview

"Fifteen percent of 240: ten percent is 24, five percent is half that, 12, so 36."

That is the whole answer. Name the blocks as you go, so the interviewer can follow, then say what the number means: "So the fee costs them $36M a year, which is more than their entire marketing budget."

Three tricks that save time

Flip the percentage

x% of y is the same as y% of x. 4% of 75 is awkward; 75% of 4 is 3. Use whichever way round is easier.

Use fractions you know

12.5% is one eighth, 33.3% is one third, 20% is one fifth. 12.5% of 640 is 640 ÷ 8 = 80. The case maths cheat sheet has the full fraction table.

Work backwards by dividing, not subtracting

If a price is $60 after a 20% increase, the original was $60 ÷ 1.2 = $50, not $60 − 20% = $48. The percentage applied to the original, so you have to undo it the same way.

Points versus percent: the trap that changes the answer

A retailer has sales of $240M a year and pays delivery fees of 15% of sales, so $36M. Management wants to cut that rate to 12%.

  • The saving is 3 percentage points of sales: 3% of $240M = $7.2M a year, before any cost of making the change and assuming sales stay flat.
  • In relative terms, the fee rate falls by 3 ÷ 15 = 20%. Check: 20% of $36M is also $7.2M.

Both statements are true, but they sound very different. "We cut delivery costs by 3%" undersells it; "we cut them by 20%" is accurate if you mean the fee itself. Say "percentage points" when you mean the difference between two rates, and "percent" when you mean a relative change.

Common mistakes

  • Calculating 15% as 0.15 × 240 by long multiplication under pressure. The block method is faster and harder to fumble.
  • Adding successive percentages. A 20% rise followed by a 20% fall leaves you at 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, a 4% loss, not back where you started.
  • Using the wrong base. "Up 25%" and "down 20%" can describe the same gap ($80 to $100, or $100 to $80). Say which number you are measuring from.

Practice

1. What is 17.5% of 360?

Show the answer

10% is 36, 5% is 18, 2.5% is 9. Total 36 + 18 + 9 = 63.

2. After a 25% discount, a jacket costs $45. What was the full price?

Show the answer

$45 is 75% of the original, so $45 ÷ 0.75 = $60. Check: 25% of $60 is $15, and $60 − $15 = $45.

3. A bank's cost-to-income ratio falls from 60% to 55%. Describe the change two ways.

Show the answer

It fell by 5 percentage points, which is a relative fall of 5 ÷ 60 = 8.3%. On $1B of income, that is $50M a year less cost.

Where to practise next

Percentages appear in almost every exhibit, so practise them on charts in the chart reading drill and in timed sums in the case maths drill. For margin percentages, which have their own trap, read margin vs markup.
